query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing lattice distortion at the FCC/BCC interfaces in the as-deposited high‐entropy alloy coating enhances dislocation pinning, thereby reducing creep deformation under continuous loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited FCC/BCC high‐entropy alloy protective coating exhibiting standard lattice coherency and moderate lattice distortion at phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Adjust deposition parameters (e.g., increase substrate temperature or alter sputtering power) or introduce minor compositional tweaks to specifically enhance lattice distortion and reduce interfacial coherency at the FCC/BCC boundaries while keeping overall composition constant.
generation.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading under moderate-to-high temperature conditions that simulate service environments where creep is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of lattice distortion and interfacial coherency at the FCC/BCC (or similar FCC/B2) phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion at the phase boundaries increases the pinning of dislocations, thereby hindering their motion during continuous stress. This increased dislocation impediment delays progressive plastic deformation (creep) relative to the baseline microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings modified to increase lattice distortion will exhibit a lower creep rate, evidenced by reduced dislocation mobility and delayed onset of tertiary creep, compared to the standard as-deposited coating.
generation.baseline: The standard, as‐deposited coating with typical lattice distortion and interfacial characteristics.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under stress and temperature regimes that do not induce additional phase transformations or severe microstructural instabilities; beyond these regimes, other mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exclusive influence of lattice distortion, as other microstructural factors (e.g., grain size, incidental phase precipitates) may also affect creep behavior. Further isolation of this variable is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one using standard deposition conditions (baseline) and another with adjusted parameters to systematically enhance lattice distortion at FCC/BCC interfaces. Subject both sets to identical sustained creep tests at designed moderate-to-high temperatures and loads. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the degree of lattice distortion and dislocation arrangements at phase boundaries.
measurements: Creep rate and strain evolution under continuous loading
Dislocation density and spatial distribution at FCC/BCC interfaces (via TEM)
Quantitative evaluation of lattice distortion at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified coatings with increased lattice distortion do not show a statistically significant decrease in creep rate or evidence of enhanced dislocation pinning relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that increased lattice distortion at the phase boundaries governs the improved creep resistance is refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
Data Availability Statement

The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

frame.system: An FCC/BCC high‐entropy-alloy protective coating in its as-deposited state that is known to undergo progressive plastic deformation under continuous loading.
frame.goal: To elucidate and test the mechanistic origin of the coating’s creep resistance, specifically by identifying the influence of microstructural features (such as lattice distortion, phase boundary effects, and local dislocation interactions) on resisting creep deformation.
frame.limitation: Under sustained loading, the coating displays progressive plastic deformation, and the exact mechanisms that limit creep are unclear.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy alloys have explored the interplay between dislocation mechanisms and phase boundaries under extreme deformation conditions. For instance, atomistic and high-pressure treatments in dual‐phase HEAs (e.g., Al0.7CoCrFeNi with FCC and ordered B2 phases in PMC11087546 and the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in PMC12806431) highlighted that interphase coherency and lattice distortion can crucially affect strength and creep/potential embrittlement. Initial simulation and rapid solidification research demonstrated that deformation and dynamic phase interactions (such as dislocation pinning at phase interfaces) modulate mechanical response. Subsequent experimental work using processing adjustments (HPHT treatments, controlled annealing) further indicated that modifying microstructural features—especially the nature of FCC/BCC (or B2) interfacial boundaries—can alter creep behavior. The trend, however, has not yet isolated how lattice distortion at the phase interfaces in as-deposited protective coatings limits progressive plastic deformation under continuous loading.
decision.unsolved: Despite recognizing that phase boundary effects and dislocation interactions underpin creep resistance in complex HEAs, it remains untested how controlled variations in the lattice distortion at FCC/BCC interfaces directly modulate creep resistance in coatings. The isolated influence of interfacial coherency, and consequently its role as the governing factor in resisting sustained stress‐induced plasticity, is still unresolved.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the lattice distortion at the FCC/BCC (or FCC/B2) phase boundaries by using targeted minor compositional tweaks or adjusting deposition parameters (such as substrate temperature or sputtering power) to modify interfacial coherency while maintaining overall composition constant. Perform creep tests under sustained moderate to high temperature stress and compare the resulting creep rates and dislocation patterns relative to a baseline as-deposited coating.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on previous findings that phase boundary properties influence dislocation pinning and creep resistance. By designing a controlled experiment that isolates the effect of lattice distortion at interfaces, the study addresses the gap in understanding the governing factor behind the coating’s creep resistance. Observing significantly altered creep behavior (or not) will serve as a clear test of the mechanistic hypothesis and provide a definitive falsification criterion if the expected trends are not met.
